The fertilised eggs of Solea senegalensis are small and planktonic, with a diameter of 0.1 cm , and they carry a modest initial endowment of 1 joule  of reserve energy to support development through the endotrophic phase. At a water temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C], hatching occurs at approximately 1.58 days , releasing a yolk-sac larva measuring 0.1382 cm  in total length at hatching. The dry weight of the freshly spawned egg is 0.00004615 grams , and by the moment of eclosion, the non-feeding prolarva has a dry mass of 33.19 micrograms . This period of lecithotrophic nutrition is brief, as the yolk is progressively consumed to fuel early morphogenesis before the critical transition to exogenous feeding.

The yolk-sac larva continues its development under the same thermal regime of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C], and mouth opening, a key event marking the onset of first exogenous feeding, occurs at 3.6 days [ab = 3.6 days]. This milestone, also termed the age at birth, is accompanied by a total length of 0.2484 cm [Lb = 0.2484 cm] and a dry weight of approximately 35.4 micrograms . The relatively low dry mass at mouth opening, only slightly greater than the value at hatching, underscores the minimal somatic growth achieved during the exclusively yolk-dependent phase. Following this trophic switch, the actively feeding larva embarks on a period of rapid growth as an exogenously feeding, free-swimming larva within the pelagic environment, building the biomass necessary for the profound morphological reorganization that lies ahead.

After about 16 days , at a sustained temperature of 19.5 °C [T = 19.5 °C], the pelagic larva attains a total length of 0.6857 cm  at the start of metamorphosis, marking the initiation of the dramatic larval-juvenile transition. By this point, the actively growing exotrophic larva has accumulated a dry weight of 553.4 micrograms , representing a substantial increase from the mass at first feeding and reflecting the intense feeding activity of the pre-metamorphic ichthyoplankton. This allometric shift involves a complete body plan reorganisation, including the migration of one eye to the contralateral side, as the fish prepares for its benthic settlement. The metamorphic climax itself is energetically demanding and typically concludes within a few days, after which the post-metamorphic juvenile adopts a demersal lifestyle on soft-bottom substrates typical of coastal and estuarine nursery grounds.

Sexual maturation in Senegalese sole is strongly size-dependent and differs between the sexes, with females achieving a total length of 38 cm [Lp = 38 cm] at puberty while males reach the same developmental milestone at a smaller length of 33 cm [Lp = 33 cm]. Correspondingly, the wet weights at puberty are 850 grams [Wwp = 850 grams] for females and 650 grams [Wwp = 650 grams] for males, a sexual size dimorphism that is common among flatfishes and likely reflects the higher energetic demands of egg production in females. The ultimate wet weight of reproductively active adults averages 1830 grams [Wwi = 1830 grams], a figure representing the mean asymptotic body mass of both sexes combined. In terms of body length, the ultimate total length for the species is 52 cm [Li = 52 cm], although exceptional individuals, particularly large females occasionally recorded in commercial catches, can approach 70 cm, highlighting the plasticity of asymptotic size under variable environmental conditions.

Reproduction in Senegalese sole is tied to the thermal regime of the Tagus estuary, where an average annual water temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C] defines the local environmental context. Under these conditions, first reproduction occurs at 4 years after hatching [tR = 4 years after hatching], a relatively late onset for a flatfish of moderate body size, possibly constrained by the need to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves for high fecundity at a temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C]. During the spawning season, females exhibit a maximum spawning rate of 4160 eggs per day [Ri = 4160 eggs per day] when measured at 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C], a temperature that falls within the optimal range for gamete release. The species is relatively long-lived for its size, with a maximum documented lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] under the same average thermal conditions, allowing multiple reproductive events over a protracted adult life that contributes to population stability at a temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C].
